Recorded as INDIRECT because the step is not demonstrated: the source that describes both ends says there is a gap between them. The edge is drawn so the graph reaches the clinical syndrome, and the gap is a discussion rather than a hidden assumption.

Headache with the ataxia is what marks the tiers in which the cerebellum is swollen. No cited source states the mechanism, so the edge is drawn through unknown intermediates: raised pressure in the posterior fossa is the obvious route and none of these papers measures it.
The other half of the pair that marks those tiers, and on the same footing: an association the cited sources report without measuring what lies between.

Swelling in the posterior fossa obstructs cerebrospinal fluid outflow. A review gives hydrocephalus or tonsillar herniation as a frequent complication of the swelling; one series describes triventricular hydrocephalus from extrinsic compression of the aqueduct of Sylvius without saying what compresses it, and one case report's CT shows the swollen hemispheres compressing the fourth ventricle, with obstructive hydrocephalus.

The swollen cerebellum, confined in the posterior fossa, pushes the tonsils down and can press on the brainstem. A review gives tonsillar herniation as a complication of the swelling, beside hydrocephalus rather than after it, and one case report's CT shows the swollen hemispheres compressing the fourth ventricle and the brainstem.

The swelling and the hydrocephalus it causes are the evident route to raised pressure, but no cited source says how the pressure rises or measures it: one series names compression of the posterior fossa, acute hydrocephalus and intracranial hypertension together as the causes of death in the fulminant form.

Two of the three child deaths from cerebellitis that the cited sources report case by case are attributed in their cached abstracts to the brainstem: one child died because of brainstem involvement, and in a three-child series the child who died had presented with obstructive hydrocephalus and progressed to brainstem failure; neither abstract says the dead child's brainstem was herniated or compressed, or that the death was sudden. For the 13-year-old who died suddenly, a later case report restates that she had brainstem compression and obstructive hydrocephalus on imaging and deteriorated rapidly to death. Two case reports also say the disease can be fatal through tonsillar herniation, hydrocephalus or brainstem compression, one of them citing earlier work. No cited source says how the compression causes death, so the edge is drawn through unknown intermediates.

Chickenpox is one of the infections that precede the syndrome. Counted from the syndrome's side, it came before a third of the cases in the Dutch national surveillance study; counted from the virus's side, acute cerebellar ataxia was the commonest neurological complication of the virus in a children's hospital series.

Epstein-Barr virus infection is one of the infections that precede the syndrome. In both adult reports the virus was found in the blood while testing of the cerebrospinal fluid for it was negative; the authors of one favour a post-infectious reading and add that serology is not the best test.
Drawn without an effect predicate. The work-up of one child found the virus, which places it beside the syndrome but does not show that it was the trigger.
Drawn without an effect predicate. The one case cited carried a second virus at the same time.

Drawn without an effect predicate. A pooled review counts influenza among the identified triggers and a hospital series found it in one child, but the two cited influenza case reports read their own case as active or direct infection.
SARS-CoV-2 infection is one of the infections that precede the syndrome: by a mean of about 15 days in one review's cases, and by nine weeks in one patient.

Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection is one of the infections that precede the syndrome, and the review of its manifestations outside the lungs places cerebellitis, as most likely, among the indirect, immune-mediated ones.
Mumps is one of the infections that precede the syndrome, in one series.

Acts on the varicella share of the preceding infections only; it has no bearing on the other triggers. No cited source measures the syndrome's incidence before and after a vaccination programme, so the effect rests on a projection from two rates, on a fall in the neurological complications of varicella as a whole, and on what is seen in a vaccinated population.
Drawn without an effect predicate: the reports place vaccination before onset, and a review of them judges causality unproved.

nodes.description: The humoral arm of the immune response, as far as it can be measured: antibodies in serum or cerebrospinal fluid that bind brain tissue or named neural antigens. The targets differ between patients and studies: glutamate receptor delta 2, a receptor of the Purkinje cell, in single cases; centrosome proteins, pericentrin among them, after varicella; and neuronal, glial and myelin antigens in 10 of 36 children with acute cerebellitis in one multicentre series. No study of this disease cited here found a single neural antigen targeted in most of its patients. Antibodies against centrosome proteins are found after varicella without ataxia as well, though not those against pericentrin. Whether any of them injures the cerebellum, rather than marking an injury already done, is not settled; the node has no edge onward for that reason, and the question is recorded in the discussions.

Cerebellar oedema in the posterior fossa obstructs cerebrospinal fluid flow and compresses the brainstem, and it is what the surgical treatments act on. nodes.description: The treatment for the swelling's hydrocephalus and mass effect, needed above all in the fulminant tier, and the one whose timing the cited three-child series turns on. External ventricular drainage or a shunt relieves the hydrocephalus; posterior fossa decompression relieves the mass effect itself. Of nine children seen by one centre's neurosurgical service, four needed external ventricular drainage, for a mean of 11 days, and none needed further surgery; in another series of nine children one needed surgery for triventricular hydrocephalus; a 7-year-old needed emergency drainage for life-threatening hydrocephalus; a 12-year-old boy recovered completely within two weeks of a ventriculoperitoneal shunt and treatment for raised pressure, and his authors call the ventricular decompression life-saving; both children of a two-child report of the fulminant form were given cerebrospinal fluid diversion; in a three-child series one girl recovered fully after emergency posterior fossa decompression when steroids had not stopped her decline; a child with para-infectious cerebellar swelling and herniation was well 3 years after an emergency posterior fossa decompression with external ventricular drainage and steroids; a 15-year-old with pseudotumoral hemicerebellitis was asymptomatic at follow-up after a decompressive craniectomy; and of two children with herniation and hydrocephalus, one was drained and the other treated without surgery, and both recovered fully.

nodes.description: Cognitive and behavioural difficulties after the acute illness, reported in series of acute cerebellar ataxia and of acute cerebellitis and measured in different ways. In a series of acute cerebellar ataxia, a fifth of the children followed for more than four months had transient behavioural or intellectual difficulties, but only 5 of 60 had sustained learning problems. In 11 children with acute cerebellitis followed for an average of 4 years and 4 months, a parental questionnaire found cognitive deficits in 6, affecting spatial visualisation, language skills and concentration, and in a series of 15 children with acute cerebellitis memory difficulties accompanied residual ataxia at a median of 12 months. In a series of children with cerebellitis for whom a neurosurgical service was consulted, cognitive impairment was the commonest residual deficit. A review of hemicerebellitis, which it calls a rare disorder of unknown origin, notes that a minority of children may show persisting fine motor or neurocognitive sequelae.

nodes.description: The commonest treatment in the pooled literature, at three quarters of patients, given on the reasoning that the disease is immune-mediated. Many of the cited sources never mention a steroid, clinical series among them. No cited source compares it against no treatment in a controlled design. The treated-against-untreated contrasts are two children in a fulminant case report, about immunomodulatory therapy rather than steroids specifically, and a series of six children whose ataxia began during acute COVID-19, one given corticosteroids and the others no specific treatment, all of whom recovered completely; their onset during the infection puts them at the border of this entry. In a series of 15 children with acute cerebellitis, 14 had steroids, and its authors suggest that steroid treatment can increase the chance of recovery, without a comparison group. Two patients of a review of Purkinje cell antibodies in autoimmune cerebellar ataxia, both with glutamate receptor delta2 antibodies, point both ways: methylprednisolone with immunoglobulin failed in the first child reported with these antibodies, and the second patient recovered without sequelae within 3 weeks of methylprednisolone. In the review's third patient, ataxia improved spontaneously and gradually, then worsened again after vaccination against mumps and varicella zoster, by the review's account.

nodes.description: A second immunotherapy, given to 19 of 73 pooled patients; in two series of acute cerebellitis it went to 8 of 15 children, 14 of whom had steroids, and to 6 of 9, all of whom had steroids. A case-based systematic review of cerebellitis after COVID-19 says that it is prescribed in all cases that do not respond to corticosteroids and that all of them improved, and that its efficacy against post-COVID cerebellitis remains unconfirmed. No cited source compares it by name with steroids alone or with no treatment (the treated child of a fulminant case report's treated-against-untreated pair received immunomodulatory therapy that its abstract does not name), and the three single cases cited point both ways. The first child reported with glutamate receptor delta2 antibodies, a 20-month-old, as a review of Purkinje cell antibodies in autoimmune cerebellar ataxia recounts, was given immunoglobulin and methylprednisolone, which failed to ameliorate the symptoms; they were still present two years later. Of the trigger, the review says only that all reported cases of cerebellar ataxia with glutamate receptor delta2 antibodies were preceded or accompanied by infection or vaccination. A 6-year-old boy with influenza A, on oseltamivir from the day the virus was found, was given immunoglobulin on day 4, and his ataxic gait had resolved within 13 days of presentation; his authors read the illness as active influenza infection although influenza was not found in his cerebrospinal fluid, and that reading puts him at this entry's border. A 22-year-old woman with an isolated pancerebellar syndrome after an upper respiratory tract infection, later found to have anti-GQ1b antibodies, was given immunoglobulin with no other treatment named; her symptoms were moderately improved by discharge on hospital day 5 and fully resolved several months later, and her authors read the case as extending the anti-GQ1b antibody syndrome, which puts her at this entry's border with that syndrome. In none of the three cases can immunoglobulin be separated from the natural course, and in the first two not from the other drug given with it (methylprednisolone in one, oseltamivir in the other).

evidence.reference_title: Microglia-Triggered Plasticity of Intrinsic Excitability Modulates Psychomotor Behaviors in Acute Cerebellar Inflammation.
evidence.snippet: Activated microglia via exposure to bacterial endotoxin lipopolysaccharide or heat-killed Gram-negative bacteria induce a potentiation of the intrinsic excitability in Purkinje neurons, which is suppressed by microglia-activity inhibitor and microglia depletion.

nodes.description: Reported rarely before onset, and causality is unproved. In a 1994 series the ataxia was related to immunisation in 3% of 73 consecutive children. A case report describes onset in a 7-month-old within 24 hours of a meningococcal B vaccine, and its review of six published cases after vaccination - among them onset within 24 hours of a meningococcal group C conjugate vaccine and ten days after varicella vaccination, with influenza, hepatitis B, human papillomavirus and DTP vaccines in the others - gives a mean interval of 6.8 days and complete recovery in each. Its authors rate their own case as probably vaccine-associated by WHO criteria, but judge causality unproved and consider an unknown infection still possible, infection being the commonest identified cause at that age; the infant had also had fever and vomiting, resolved by admission. A Dutch national study found no association with MMR, and an Australian national series found no case temporally related to any childhood vaccine.

evidence.reference_title: Course and outcome of acute cerebellar ataxia.
evidence.snippet: Twenty-six percent had chickenpox, 52% had other illnesses that were presumed to be viral, and in 3% the ataxia was related to immunization.

evidence.reference_title: Acute cerebellar ataxia following meningococcal group C conjugate vaccination.
evidence.snippet: In this patient, cerebellar symptoms started within 24 hours from the vaccination, and infective causes have been ruled out by serum and liquoral analyses.

evidence.reference_title: Early acute cerebellar ataxia after meningococcal B vaccine: a case report of a 7-month-old infant and a review of the literature.
evidence.snippet: we describe a 7-month-old female that presented ACA within 24 h from the MenB second dose vaccination.

evidence.reference_title: Acute cerebellar ataxia with abnormal MRI lesions after varicella vaccination.
evidence.snippet: A 2-year-old boy, with the primary difficulties of nausea and vomiting, developed a staggering gait and dysarthria 10 days after varicella vaccination.

evidence.reference_title: Early acute cerebellar ataxia after meningococcal B vaccine: a case report of a 7-month-old infant and a review of the literature.
evidence.snippet: Overall, considering the hypothesis of an immune mediated reaction to vaccine components and after exclusion of other causes, vaccination can be considered as a possible trigger of ACA, although it cannot be proved, and it cannot be classified as certain cause.

evidence.reference_title: Acute cerebellar ataxia in the Netherlands: a study on the association with vaccinations and varicella zoster infection.
evidence.snippet: We found no association with MMR, but chickenpox was clearly related to ACA.

evidence.reference_title: Postinfectious Acute Cerebellar Syndromes in Children: A Nationally Ascertained Case Series From Australia 2013-2018.
evidence.snippet: A total of 20 cases (65% were vaccinated for varicella) were included, of which 70% were subcategorized as acute cerebellar ataxia (ACA), 20% acute cerebellitis (AC), and 10% acute fulminant cerebellitis (AFC). An acute febrile illness was noted in 55% and none were related to varicella or were temporally related to varicella vaccination or other childhood vaccines.

nodes.description: Protects against the varicella share of the syndrome. In a national Australian surveillance series from a population with high vaccine coverage, none of 20 cases followed varicella. The vaccine itself is reported before onset far more rarely than the infection: a Dutch study sets a reporting rate of 0.15 per 100,000 vaccine doses against 5 cases per 100,000 infections in young children, though its abstract does not say where the per-dose figure was measured.

nodes.description: Chickenpox, the primary infection with varicella-zoster virus. Before varicella vaccination it was the infection most often identified before the syndrome, in about a quarter of children in large series. The syndrome follows only a small fraction of infections: a Dutch surveillance study put it at 5 cases per 100,000 infections in children up to 5 years.

evidence.reference_title: Acute cerebellar ataxia in the Netherlands: a study on the association with vaccinations and varicella zoster infection.
evidence.snippet: We found no association with MMR, but chickenpox was clearly related to ACA. According to age-specific seroprevalence data the incidence rate of ACA was 5:100,000 VZV infections for children up to 5 years, compared to an ACA-reporting rate of 0.15:100,000 doses VZV-vaccine.
